defects.description: Order Intake Function [N4] writes to Order Store [N5] and separately publishes to Order Events Topic [N6] without a transactional outbox; if the SNS publish fails or the function crashes after the DynamoDB write succeeds, downstream order steps are silently lost.

Order API [N3] is configured as an API Gateway HTTP API (apiType: HTTP) with a direct read edge to Order Store [N5] (DynamoDB), but API Gateway HTTP APIs do not support direct DynamoDB service integrations.
Order API [N3] sets authorizer: n17, which references Observability [N17] (Amazon CloudWatch) instead of User Pool [N2] (Amazon Cognito), leaving the Cognito User Pool node completely disconnected.

Payment DLQ [N8], Inventory DLQ [N11], Email DLQ [N14], and Observability [N17] have no edges in the diagram, leaving the dead-letter queues disconnected from their source SQS queues and unmonitored by CloudWatch alarms.

Requirements R8, R9, and R10 are left as raw clarifying questions instead of stated assumptions, and Payment Processor [N9] and Inventory Processor [N12] lack outbound edges to payment or inventory targets.

reviews.summary: Design A uses an appropriate SNS-to-SQS fan-out pattern for independent order processing, but suffers from a dual-write reliability gap at order intake, an unsupported direct HTTP API-to-DynamoDB integration, a misreferenced API authorizer ID, and disconnected DLQ and observability nodes.

defects.description: Orders API [N2] specifies a Cognito authorizer in its configuration and rationale, but no Amazon Cognito node is modeled in the diagram.

The SNS topic [N7] and SQS queues [N6, N8-N13] do not explicitly specify encryption at rest in their node configurations, and the downstream workers do not update order status back in Orders table [N4].

reviews.summary: Design B delivers a resilient, production-grade event-driven architecture that prevents silent event loss using DynamoDB Streams as a transactional outbox with an on-failure queue, isolates downstream steps with SQS queues and DLQs, enforces idempotency, and alarms on all failure queues.

defects.description: Requirements R6 and R7 are written as raw clarifying questions in the requirements list rather than declarative requirement statements, although the chosen targets (500 TPS and 99.95% availability) are stated in the node rationales.

No data pipeline is shown to export or curate historical transactions from Transactions Table [N6] into Model Artifacts & Training Data Bucket [N7] for monthly retraining, and Retraining Workflow [N9] does not explicitly mention a model evaluation gate before updating the live endpoint.

reviews.summary: Design A presents a clean, well-connected serverless checkout and SageMaker real-time inference architecture with automated monthly retraining via EventBridge and Step Functions.

defects.description: Checkout scoring function [N5] is placed inside a private VPC subnet (Private subnet AZ1 [C6]) and must reach Transactions table [N7] (DynamoDB), CloudWatch [N13], and Fraud model endpoint [N6], but Checkout VPC [C3] has no NAT Gateway and no VPC Endpoints (for DynamoDB, SageMaker Runtime, or CloudWatch Logs), leaving the function unable to reach regional AWS services.

Checkout scoring function [N5] is placed only in Private subnet AZ1 [C6] and Fraud model endpoint [N6] is placed only in Private subnet AZ2 [C7], creating a single-AZ failure domain for Lambda that violates R12 and AWS multi-AZ best practices.

Read edges from ML artifacts and training data bucket [N9] to SageMaker training job [N12] and Fraud model endpoint [N6] are inverted (depicting S3 initiating connections to SageMaker), and requirements R9 and R10 are left as raw questions.

reviews.summary: Design B adds good security controls such as WAF and KMS customer-managed keys, but places the checkout Lambda function into a single-AZ private subnet without VPC endpoints or a NAT Gateway, breaking connectivity to DynamoDB and CloudWatch and undermining multi-AZ availability.

defects.description: Although Portal VPC [C3] defines Public subnet B [C7] and Private subnet B [C9] in Availability Zone B [C5], Application Load Balancer [N6], NAT Gateway [N7], and AWS Fargate tasks [N10] are placed exclusively in AZ A, leaving AZ B empty; ALBs require subnets in at least two AZs and single-AZ NAT/compute placement violates R12.

Under R4 (all data encrypted at rest with customer-controlled keys), Amazon RDS [N14] and Audit and log archive bucket [N17] configure KMS encryption, but Amazon ECR [N11], AWS Secrets Manager [N12], and Amazon CloudWatch [N15] do not explicitly specify KMS encryption in their configurations.

Supporting nodes AWS Shield [N3], AWS Certificate Manager [N5], Amazon ECS [N9], and AWS KMS [N13] have no edges in the diagram, and the edge from Retail customer [N1] to Amazon Route 53 [N2] is labeled HTTPS instead of DNS.

reviews.summary: Design A covers the full regulated banking portal stack—including WAF, Shield, ACM, ALB, Cognito with MFA, Fargate in private subnets with NAT egress, Secrets Manager, RDS Multi-AZ with KMS, and CloudTrail—with its main flaw being that compute and network nodes are placed only in AZ A while leaving AZ B subnets empty.

defects.description: API tasks [N11, N12] run on AWS Fargate in private subnets [C6, C7] and send logs to Amazon CloudWatch [N16], but Portal VPC [C3] has no NAT Gateway, no VPC Endpoints (for ECR, S3, or CloudWatch Logs), and no ECR repository, so tasks cannot pull container images or publish logs.

Design B states that customers sign in directly to Amazon Cognito [N8] and pass customer identity tokens on API requests through CloudFront [N2] to HTTPS application load balancer [N9] for ALB Cognito/OIDC authentication; however, ALB authenticate-cognito uses browser redirects and session cookies rather than validating bearer tokens on stateless API requests.

The architecture completely omits any database or persistent application data store for customer accounts and portal API data, despite R1 (self-service portal API), R4 (encrypt all data at rest with bank-controlled keys), and R10 (customer data retention).

HTTPS application load balancer [N9] is internet-facing in a public subnet while AWS WAF [N3] is only attached to CloudFront [N2], with no origin access restriction (such as CloudFront VPC origins, prefix lists, or custom header validation with ALB WAF) to stop attackers from bypassing CloudFront and WAF.

HTTPS application load balancer [N9] is placed only in Public subnet A [C4] while leaving Public subnet B [C5] empty, whereas an Application Load Balancer requires subnets across at least two Availability Zones.

AWS WAF [N3] and ACM certificates [N6] associated with CloudFront [N2] are placed in Bank selected AWS Region [C2], whereas CloudFront WAF web ACLs and ACM certificates must be provisioned in us-east-1.
Requirements R8, R9, and R10 are left as raw clarifying questions, and there are two duplicate edges from CloudFront [N2] to HTTPS application load balancer [N9].

reviews.summary: Design B omits any database for customer portal data, isolates private-subnet Fargate tasks without NAT Gateways or VPC endpoints so they cannot pull images or ship logs, and relies on an unworkable ALB Cognito bearer-token authentication pattern behind CloudFront.

preference.why: Design B avoids the dual-write event-loss risk of Design A by using DynamoDB Streams with an on-failure queue as a transactional outbox, properly connects all DLQs and downstream targets, and models idempotency and DLQ alarms.

Design A provides a complete, working serverless and SageMaker architecture, whereas Design B places the checkout Lambda function in a single-AZ private subnet without VPC endpoints or a NAT Gateway, breaking DynamoDB and CloudWatch connectivity and multi-AZ availability.

Design A includes the complete application and data stack (including RDS Multi-AZ, Secrets Manager, ECR, and NAT Gateway), whereas Design B omits a database entirely, lacks NAT/VPC endpoints for private Fargate tasks, and misuses ALB Cognito authentication for bearer-token API calls.
